land.text: the Byzantine theme of Nicopolis: 'the lands between Dyrrhachium (Durazzo) in the north and Naupactus in the south', taken over by Michael Komnenos Doukas from Arta in 1205
Dyrrhachium (Venetian from 1205, taken by Michael I probably in 1213) and Corfu (Venetian from 1207, taken in 1214)

predecessors.note: Not at birth: the two Venetian holdings were taken in 1213-1214.

land.text: Vonitsa and the Ionian islands (Lefkada, Cephalonia, Zakynthos, Ithaca), which 'quickly fell to the Ottomans in August and September 1479'

successors.note: Earlier Ottoman takes: Ioannina 9 October 1430, Arta 24 March 1449, Angelokastro 1460. Venice took Zakynthos from the Ottomans in 1482 and kept Cephalonia after 1500.

land.text: Epirus proper (Arta 1338, Ioannina 1335/36, Thomokastron 1340), annexed by Andronikos III

successors.note: The 1337-1340 annexation ended the first despotate; the state was restored in 1356 and at Ioannina from 1367, so the Byzantine handover is intermediate, not final.

land.text: Thessalonica and Thessaly, kept by Manuel Komnenos Doukas as a Bulgarian vassal after Klokotnitsa (1230)

successors.note: An intermediate split in 1230, not a final successor.

land.text: Thessaly 'from Mount Olympus in the north to Mount Parnassus in the south', John I Doukas' share at the partition of 1268

capitals.name: Thessalonica (Thessaloniki)
capitals.note: Infobox: Thessalonica 1227-1230, Theodore's imperial capital after his coronation.

capitals.name: Arta
capitals.note: Nikephoros II's restored despotate (1356-1359); the infobox gives Ioannina 1356-1430, but Nikephoros chased Simeon Uros from Arta.

capitals.name: Ioannina
capitals.note: Infobox: Ioannina 1356-1430; the Despotate of Ioannina of Thomas Preljubovic, Esau de' Buondelmonti and Carlo I Tocco. Ottoman from 9 October 1430.

capitals.name: Vonitsa
capitals.note: Infobox: Vonitsa 1460-1479; Leonardo III in practice ruled from Lefkada.

rulers.name: Theodore Komnenos Doukas
rulers.note: Ruler of Epirus 1215-1230; Emperor of Thessalonica 1224-1230; captured at Klokotnitsa.

rulers.name: Thomas I Komnenos Doukas
rulers.note: Under the regency of his mother Anna; murdered by Nicholas Orsini 1318.

rulers.name: Nikephoros II Orsini
rulers.note: Under Anna's regency; infobox 1335-1340; Byzantine annexation 1337-1340.

rulers.name: Nikephoros II Orsini (restored)
rulers.note: Ruler of Thessaly and Epirus 1356-1359; killed at Achelous.

rulers.name: Simeon Uros
rulers.title: Serbian emperor at Trikala, nominal lord of Epirus
rulers.note: The Epirote towns 'quickly submitted to his rule' in 1359 but the countryside was Albanian; he governed through deputies.

rulers.name: Carlo I Tocco
rulers.note: Invited to Ioannina February 1411; despot 1415; died 4 July 1429.

rulers.name: Carlo II Tocco
rulers.note: Ottoman vassal from 1430; died October 1448 (Leonardo III page: 30 September 1448).

rulers.name: Leonardo III Tocco
rulers.note: Reign 30 September 1448 - September 1479; titular in exile to c. 1503.

correction.text: the theme of Nicopolis 'between Dyrrhachium (Durazzo) in the north and Naupactus in the south' as Michael took it over in 1205, Dyrrhachium itself and Corfu excepted (Venetian 1205/1207-1213/14)

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe: the state begins in 1205, Cliopatria's first shape in 1206.

correction.text: the shape without Dyrrhachium (Venetian 1205-1213) and Corfu (Venetian 1207-1214); Thessaly (Larissa) is added only in 1212

keyframe_review.note: 47,956 km2 for 1206-1215, bbox north to 42.5 N. No infobox area exists for Epirus.
68,323 km2, bbox east to 23.02 E: Thessaly (1212) and Ohrid-Prilep-Pelagonia ('by 1217 he held Ohrid, Prilep, and most of the plain of Pelagonia'); Platamon 1218.

82,729 km2 for 1220-1226: Serres (late 1221), the rest of Thessaly except Halmyros (c. 1222/23), Thessalonica and Chalkidike (December 1224), eastern Macedonia and western Thrace with Adrianople (1225). The 1225 Thracian conquests arrive in the next shape, two years late.

correction.text: as drawn (108,525 km2, Thrace 'as far east as Didymoteicho and Adrianople') until the Battle of Klokotnitsa, 9 March 1230; from then only Epirus proper, Cliopatria's own 1236 shape, since 'within a few months Thrace, most of Macedonia, and Albania, fell under Bulgarian rule' and Thessalonica with Thessaly stayed with Manuel as a Bulgarian vassal (the Empire of Thessalonica dossier)

keyframe_review.note: Cliopatria keeps Theodore's empire whole to 1235, five years after Klokotnitsa, and starts its Empire of Thessalonica row only in 1236. The 1224-1230 empire is carried here under rule 2 (rename event 1227).
41,115 km2 for 1236-1240: Michael II's Epirus proper with Corfu ('by 1236, he had seized Corfu'); Thessaly is Manuel's (1239-1241).
55,640 km2: Thessaly, occupied by Michael II on Manuel's death in 1241.

correction.text: as drawn for 1250-1251 (Albania and north-western Macedonia gained from 1246), but from the Larissa treaty of 1252 without the Macedonian holdings (Prilep, Veles, Vodena, Kastoria, Deabolis ceded to Nicaea), from 1256 without Dyrrhachium and Servia (ceded to Theodore II Laskaris; Dyrrhachium passed from Nicaea to Manfred in February 1258), from 1258 without Valona and Butrint (the Albanian coast Manfred captured) and from 1259 without Corfu (Helena's dowry); Berat is left in because no opened page says who held it

keyframe_review.note: 61,424 km2 for 1250-1271 with a bbox north to 42.11 N, which keeps northern Albania Epirote fourteen years after it was lost. The Nicaean occupation of 1259-1260 is hatched, not removed.

46,676 km2 for 1272-1278: Thessaly gone (John I Doukas' state from 1267/68; Cliopatria's Thessaly row begins 1272) and Charles of Anjou holding Dyrrhachium (1272). Nikephoros I's Epirus with the Albanian hinterland.
20,356 km2 for 1279-1293, bbox north only to 40.10 N: 'With Charles' defeat soon after [1279], Nikephoros lost his holdings in Albania to the Byzantines'; Butrint surrendered to Charles in 1279.

correction.text: without the coastal fortresses (Naupaktos, Vonitsa, Butrint) transferred to Philip of Taranto as Thamar's dowry in 1294, Epirote again 1304-1307 and ceded back 1307; from 1318 without Ioannina, which 'declared itself for the Byzantine emperor as soon as the murder of Thomas became known'

keyframe_review.note: 20,648 km2 for 1294-1325. The pages name Butrint and Naupaktos (1304-05) but not every dowry fortress; Vonitsa is the researcher's reading (confidence 2 in the ledger).

correction.text: as drawn for 1326-1335 (John II Orsini 'was allowed to establish his control over all of Epirus in exchange for recognizing Byzantine suzerainty'), with the Epirote part of Thessaly added 1332-1336; from 1336 without Ioannina and from 1338 without Arta (Andronikos III 'installed his governors in Epirus'); the Arta rebellion of late 1338 holds the south until the strongholds 'capitulated' by the end of 1340; the state is landless 1341-1355

keyframe_review.note: 18,471 km2 to 1343. The infobox dates the Byzantine conquest 1337; Monomachos' page gives Arta 1338 and the surrenders 1340. Cliopatria runs the shape to 1343 and then has no Epirote shape until 1385.

correction.text: Nikephoros II Orsini 'took over the region [Thessaly] in Spring 1356, and advanced on Epirus'; the restored despotate of Epirus and Thessaly until his death at Achelous in 1359

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe for the restoration of 1356-1359 (infobox 'Restored by Nikephoros II Orsini: 1356'). After Achelous 'Aetolia and southern Epirus were divided' between Losha (Arta) and Shpata (Angelokastron) and Thessaly went to Simeon Uros.

correction.text: Ioannina and its surrounding area (central Epirus), where Thomas Preljubovic 'arrived ... from Edessa in 1367' as Simeon Uros' governor and ruled as despot; Dryinopolis and Vagenetia added 1380-1381

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe: the Despotate of Ioannina, which Cliopatria first draws in 1385. Arta and Aetolia-Acarnania are the Albanian Despotate of Arta (sibling dossier despotate-of-arta, 1359-1416).
12,110 km2 for 1385-1394: Esau de' Buondelmonti's Ioannina, 'ruler of Ioannina and its surrounding area (central Epirus)'.
12,230 km2 for 1395-1414. In 1399 'much of his land was occupied by Zenebishi' until Esau's return in 1400 (hatched, not removed). Carlo I Tocco succeeded at Ioannina in February 1411.

14,440 km2 for 1415-1421, bbox south to 37.64 N: Cliopatria folds the Tocco county of Cephalonia, Zakynthos and Lefkada into Epirus when its House of Tocco row ends (1414); the union dates from Carlo's accession at Ioannina (1411) and his title of despot (1415). Arta surrendered in 1416.

24,478 km2 for 1422-1428, bbox east to 22.16 E: 'the Tocchi controlled all major towns in Epirus' after Arta (1416) and the Acarnanian fortresses; Glarentza in Elis bought in 1421 and handed to the Byzantines on 1 May 1428.
1429-1430: Carlo II's succession (July 1429) and the Ottoman siege of Ioannina.

13,539 km2 for 1431-1449, bbox north only to 39.51 N: Ioannina surrendered to the Ottomans on 9 October 1430; Carlo II 'continued to rule over the remnants of his principality in Epirus from Arta as an Ottoman vassal' (vassal tint, rule 4).

8,643 km2 for 1450-1458: Arta 'fell to the Ottomans on 24 March 1449' and 'all of Leonardo's mainland possessions, save for the three settlements of Vonitza, Varnazza and Angelokastro, were annexed'. Cliopatria's change is a year late.
3,091 km2 for 1459-1462: Leonardo 'lost two out of his three fortresses on the mainland, only retaining Vonitza' in 1460; Cliopatria's change is a year early.
2,063 km2: Vonitsa with Lefkada, Cephalonia, Zakynthos and Ithaca.

correction.text: the shape unchanged, ending in September 1479, when Leonardo's 'few remaining possessions quickly fell to the Ottomans in August and September 1479' and he fled from Lefkada to Taranto

keyframe_review.note: Cliopatria runs the row to 1481; the state ends in 1479 (infobox 'Ottoman conquest of Vonitsa: 1479').

region.text: the theme of Nicopolis, 'the lands between Dyrrhachium (Durazzo) in the north and Naupactus in the south', ruled from Arta

ledger.note: 1205: Michael Komnenos Doukas sets up at Arta. He 'considered himself the Byzantine governor of the old province of Nicopolis' and 'from his base at Arta, Michael proceeded to expand his control over most of the region of Epirus'. The page gives no boundary; Dyrrhachium (Venetian 1205) and Corfu (Venetian 1207) were not his.

region.text: 'Larissa and much of central Thessaly came under Epirote rule'

ledger.note: 1212: Michael I takes Larissa and central Thessaly from the Lombard lords. 'In 1212, he conquered most of Thessaly from the Lombard lords of Thessalonica' (Michael I page). Salona was held only briefly c. 1210-1212.

region.text: Dyrrhachium (Durazzo)

ledger.note: 1213: Dyrrhachium taken from Venice. 'Soon after, probably in 1213, he took Dyrrhachium from Venice, followed in 1214 by Corfu.'

region.text: the island of Corfu (Corcyra)

ledger.note: 1214: Corfu taken from Venice. The Despotate page: 'In 1214 he captured Corcyra from Venice'; the Corfu page: 'In 1214, it passed to the Greek despots of Epirus'.

region.text: Kruja and the principality of Arbanon

ledger.note: c. 1215: Arbanon absorbed. 'Michael continued to push northward into Albania and Macedonia, taking Kruja and ending the independence of the principality of Arbanon'; the page gives no year, and the attempt on Zeta 'was stopped by the Serbs at Skadar'. Cliopatria has no Arbanon row in this group's tables.

region.text: 'by 1217 he held Ohrid, Prilep, and most of the plain of Pelagonia'

ledger.note: By 1217: Theodore holds Ohrid, Prilep and Pelagonia. The page does not name the previous holder (Bulgaria, or the late Strez's lordship); the counterpart is the researcher's reading.

region.text: 'the great Platamon Castle', commanding the entrance to the Thermaic Gulf

ledger.note: 1218: Platamon surrenders. 'The surrender of the great Platamon Castle in 1218' cleared the Thermaic Gulf.

region.text: Serres

ledger.note: Late 1221: Serres surrenders. 'With the surrender of Serres in late 1221, Theodore cut the land connection between Constantinople and Thessalonica.' Whether Serres was held by the kingdom or the emperor's men is not said.

region.text: 'the entire region except for Halmyros'

ledger.note: c. 1222/23: the rest of Thessaly. Theodore 'completed the recovery of the entire region except for Halmyros' (Medieval Thessaly); the year is approximate.

region.text: Thessalonica and 'Chalcidice with Mount Athos'

ledger.note: December 1224: Thessalonica falls. 'The exhausted defenders of Thessalonica surrendered the city to Theodore sometime in December 1224'; the Latins 'could not stop' it (Despotate page). The Kingdom of Thessalonica ends.

region.text: 'eastern Macedonia and western Thrace, seizing Christopolis, Xanthi, Gratianopolis, Mosynopolis and Didymoteicho'

ledger.note: Spring 1225: Theodore overruns Latin Thrace. 'Epirote armies then conquered Thrace in 1225-26, appearing before Constantinople itself' (Latin Empire page); he reached Bizye and Vrysis but 'Constantinople itself was not attacked'.

region.text: Adrianople

ledger.note: 1225: Adrianople taken from the Nicaean garrison. The Despotate page: 'Theodore retook Adrianople from Nicaea' in 1225; the Vatatzes page dates it 1227 ('drove the Nicaean garrison out of Adrianople and annexed much of Thrace in 1227'). Cliopatria's shape changes in 1227.

1227: Theodore is crowned emperor at Thessalonica; the Epirote state is styled the Empire of Thessalonica. 'The date of his actual coronation is unknown': 1225 (Karpozilos) or 1227 (Stavridou-Zafraka 'has narrowed the date down to 29 May 1227'). Same state, same colour (rule 2); the 1230-1246 rump at Thessalonica is the empire-of-thessalonica dossier.
1227: the court sits at Thessalonica (infobox 'Thessalonica (1227-1230)').

region.text: Thessalonica and its environs with Thessaly, where 'Manuel was allowed by Ivan Asen II to rule in Thessalonica and its environs with the title of despotes'

ledger.note: 1230: the realm divides. 'Thessalonica itself became a Bulgarian vassal under Theodore's brother Manuel', while 'the original nucleus of the state, Epirus, broke free under Michael II Komnenos Doukas' (Empire of Thessalonica page). Epirus proper continues here; the Thessalonican rump is a new dossier from 1230.
c. 1230/31: Michael II rules Epirus from Arta again.

region.text: 'Thrace, most of Macedonia, and Albania'; Ivan Asen II: 'I conquered all of his land from Odrin (Adrianople) to Drach (Dyrrhachium), Greek and also Albanian and Serbian'

ledger.note: 9 March 1230: Klokotnitsa. Theodore's army 'was destroyed and he himself taken captive and later blinded'; 'within a few months Thrace, most of Macedonia, and Albania, fell under Bulgarian rule', 'although Dyrrhachium itself apparently remained in Greek hands'.

region.text: Corfu

ledger.note: By 1236: Michael II holds Corfu. 'By 1236, he had seized Corfu.' The page does not say from whom; Corfu had been Theodore's and the Thessalonican line's is the researcher's reading.

region.text: Thessaly, Manuel's domain of 1239-1241

ledger.note: 1241: Thessaly to Michael II. 'In 1241 Manuel died, Michael moved in quickly to occupy Thessaly before either of his remaining uncles could react'; 'the area quickly, and apparently without resistance' passed to him (Medieval Thessaly).

region.text: 'Albania and northwestern Macedonia' (Kastoria, Vodena, the Albanian coast as far as Dyrrhachium)

ledger.note: 1246: Michael II expands as Bulgaria crumbles. 'Michael II also took advantage of the opportunity to expand into Albania and northwestern Macedonia' (the year Vatatzes took Thessalonica and Bulgarian Macedonia). The previous holder of each town is the researcher's reading.

region.text: 'not only the fortresses he had recently captured but all his remaining holdings in Macedonia' (Prilep, Veles, Vodena, Kastoria, Deabolis), 'while Kruja would come under Vatatzes' suzerainty'

ledger.note: 1252: the treaty of Larissa. After 'capturing Prilep and Veles' in 1252 Michael withdrew; 'Vatatzes besieged and captured Vodena and took Kastoria and Deabolis in winter 1252/53' and Michael ceded his Macedonian holdings.

region.text: Dyrrhachium and Servia

ledger.note: 1256: Dyrrhachium and Servia to Nicaea. Theodore II 'forced Michael II Komnenos Doukas, the ruler of Epirus, to cede Dyrrachium on the coast of the Adriatic Sea to Nicaea', only releasing Michael's wife 'after Michael II ceded Servia and Dyrrachium to him'.

region.text: Prilep

ledger.note: 1257: Michael II revolts. 'Palaiologos' withdrawal enabled Michael II to seize Prilep and capture Akropolites, who was its governor.'

region.text: Avlona (Valona) and the coast to Butrint: the Epirote part of the 'Albania' that Manfred 'captured most of'; Dyrrhachium is left out, Nicaean since 1256

ledger.note: 1258: Manfred of Sicily takes the Epirote share of the Albanian coast. Manfred 'landed his own troops in Albania and captured most of it, as well as Corfu'; Michael II then 'offered to hand over Albania and Corfu as the dowry of his eldest daughter Helena' (wedding 2 June 1259) and in spring 1259 Avlona was 'held by his ally Manfred' (Pelagonia page); 'he was attacked by King Manfred of Sicily, who conquered Albania and Corcyra' (Despotate page). Dyrrhachium is not in this loss: Epirus ceded it to Nicaea in 1256 (/ledger/21) and Manfred 'expelled the Nicaean garrisons from Dyrrachium and other fortresses on the Adriatic by the end of February 1258' (Theodore II Laskaris page), so that hand-over is nicaean-empire's loss. No opened page says which other Adriatic fortresses were Nicaean-held; Avlona is the one place the Pelagonia page names and Butrint (Charles held it in 1267, Butrint page) is the researcher's reading; Berat is left undecided.

region.text: Corfu, 'given to Manfred of Sicily as a dowry in 1259'

ledger.note: 1259: Corfu to Manfred as Helena's dowry. 'In 1214, it passed to the Greek despots of Epirus, who gave it to Manfred of Sicily as a dowry in 1259.' Confirmed to Charles of Anjou by the Treaty of Viterbo (May 1267).

region.text: Ohrid and Deavolis (Devol) 'and other cities'

ledger.note: Spring 1259: Ohrid and Deavolis to Nicaea. 'In spring 1259, the Nicaeans went on the offensive' and, as the Epirotes retreated, 'the Nicaean generals captured Ohrid and Deavolis and other cities'. Deavolis had been ceded to Nicaea in 1252 (/ledger/20), so Epirus held it again by 1259; no opened page dates that recovery ('Epirote-Nicaean conflict (1257-59)' did not load).

region.text: Prilep

ledger.note: 1259: Prilep back to Nicaea, bridging a silence. Michael II seized Prilep in 1257 (/ledger/22); in summer 1259 'Michael II with his troops withdrew towards Prilep' before the battle, and the page says nothing of Prilep afterwards. nicaean-empire's ledger records a 1259 gain of 'Prilep and Pelagonia' from this state (citing this page, which is silent on it too), and nothing here returns Prilep to Epirus, whose 1259-1260 occupation pair covers only Cliopatria's 1250 shape and Thessaly.

region.text: Epirus and Thessaly: the Nicaeans 'captured the Epirote capital, Arta, forcing Michael II to flee to the island of Cephalonia' and 'bypassed Ioannina, which they left under siege'

ledger.note: Summer 1259: Pelagonia. After the battle ('early summer or autumn of 1259') 'the Nicaeans occupied Epirus' (Michael II page) and 'Thessaly was occupied by the Empire of Nicaea' (Medieval Thessaly); Epirus kept 'only Ioannina and Vonitsa' (Despotate page). Hatched, rule 4.

region.text: Epirus and Thessaly recovered in 'an Epirote counter-offensive in spring 1260'

ledger.note: 1260: Michael II recovers his domains. 'In the next year, however, the Nicaean successes were largely undone'; he 'recovered his domains with further help from Manfred' (Michael II page). In 1264 another defeat 'forced him to accept the nominal suzerainty of Michael VIII Palaiologos' (vassal tint from the Byzantine dossier).

region.text: Thessaly 'from Mount Olympus in the north to Mount Parnassus in the south, with the Achelous River serving as his border with Epirus proper', John I Doukas' share

ledger.note: 1267/68: the partition between Michael II's sons. 'His domains were split between his sons' Nikephoros I of Epirus and John I of Thessaly. Cliopatria's Thessaly row begins only in 1272.

region.text: Butrinto

ledger.note: 1278: Butrint retaken from the Byzantines. 'Byzantine forces re-entered Butrint' in 1274, which Nikephoros considered 'to be his domain'; Charles of Anjou and Nikephoros 'allied against Byzantine Emperor Michael, and together drove the Byzantines from the area in 1278' (Butrint page). Nikephoros I page: 'The coalition of Charles of Anjou, Nikephoros, and the latter's half-brother John I Doukas of Thessaly ... gained several cities, including Butrinto in 1278'. Charles himself had held Butrint since 1267 ('took control of both Butrint and Corfu'), so the loser is the Byzantine Empire, not Charles; Nikephoros surrendered the town to Charles in 1279 (next event).

region.text: Butrinto, surrendered to Charles

ledger.note: 1279: Nikephoros becomes Charles' vassal. 'In 1279 Nikephoros acknowledged himself Charles' vassal and surrendered Butrinto to his overlord' (vassal tint from the Angevin dossier, 1279-1281).

region.text: 'his holdings in Albania' north of the Ioannina basin (the Drinos valley, the Vjosa and the coast to Valona)

ledger.note: c. 1280-1281: northern Epirus and Albania to the Byzantines. 'With Charles' defeat soon after [1279], Nikephoros lost his holdings in Albania to the Byzantines.' The year is Cliopatria's shape change (1279); the Angevin defeat at Berat was 1281.

region.text: 'several coastal fortresses' transferred to Philip of Taranto as Thamar's dowry (Naupaktos, Vonitsa and Butrint are the researcher's reading)

ledger.note: 1294: the Taranto dowry. 'The wedding took place in 1294 and involved the transfer of several coastal fortresses to Philip as Thamar's dowry'; the Thessalian ruler seized most of them and 'most of these were recovered by the Angevins and peace was restored in 1296'. The Despotate page: Nikephoros 'sold much of his territory to Philip of Taranto' c. 1292.

region.text: Butrinto and Naupaktos

ledger.note: 1304-1305: Anna's Epirus recovers the Angevin coast. 'The Epirotes advanced into the Angevin lands in the western Balkans, recovering Butrinto and Naupaktos in 1304-1305.'

region.text: 'many of the fortresses' retaken 1304-1305, ceded back to Philip of Taranto

ledger.note: 1307: compromise with the Angevins. 'A new Angevin invasion in 1307 ended with a compromise' under which 'Philip of Taranto was ceded many of the fortresses'; 'in 1312, Philip gave up his claim to Epirus' (Despotate page).

1318: the Orsini take Epirus. Nicholas Orsini 'surprised and murdered his childless uncle, Thomas I Komnenos Doukas of Epirus' and 'easily subdued the entire southern portion of the principality around Arta'. Dynasty change, same state (rule 2).

region.text: 'the northern part of the Epirote realm, including Ioannina', which 'declared itself for the Byzantine emperor as soon as the murder of Thomas became known'

ledger.note: 1318: Ioannina goes over to Byzantium. Nicholas received the title of despot 'in 1319/20 in exchange for Nicholas' pledge to recognize the loss of Ioannina'; 'his rule was limited to Akarnania' (Despotate page).

region.text: 'all of Epirus', including the Ioannina basin, under Byzantine suzerainty

ledger.note: c. 1325: John II Orsini recovers the north as a Byzantine despot. After 1324 he 'was allowed to establish his control over all of Epirus in exchange for recognizing Byzantine suzerainty' and was 'awarded the title of despotes by the Byzantine emperor'. The page names no town and no year; Ioannina was Byzantine again by 1335 (Monomachos page), so the extent of this recovery is a gap.

region.text: 'the island of Leucas and the mainland castle of Vonitsa'

ledger.note: August 1331: Walter VI of Brienne's expedition. Sailing from Brindisi in August he attacked Cephalonia and Epirus 'forcing them to recognize the overlordship of King Robert' and 'seized the island of Leucas and the mainland castle of Vonitsa for himself'; 'when Walter besieged Arta, John was forced to accept Angevin suzerainty' (John II page). Walter held Lefkada and Vonitsa as a Neapolitan vassal and enfeoffed them to Graziano Zorzi in 1355.

region.text: western Thessaly ('the Epirote part of Thessaly'); the Byzantines 'asserted control over at least the eastern portion of the region'

ledger.note: 1332: John II invades Thessaly. 'In 1332, John felt strong enough to invade and annex Thessaly' after Stephen Gabrielopoulos' death; the Thessaly page gives 1332, Gabrielopoulos' page 1332/3 and the Despotate page 1333.

region.text: 'the Epirote part of Thessaly' and Ioannina

ledger.note: 1335-1336: Andronikos III closes in. He 'invaded and annexed the Epirote part of Thessaly in 1336 and advanced on Ioannina'; Byzantine forces had 'captured Ioannina by the time of John II Orsini's death in 1335' (Monomachos page).

region.text: Epirus proper with Arta: 'Epirus came peacefully under imperial rule'

ledger.note: 1337: the Byzantine annexation (infobox 'Byzantine conquest: 1337'). Andronikos III 'summoned Anna to negotiate in 1338' and 'installed his governors in Epirus'; Monomachos' page has him 'capturing the Epirote capital, Arta, and annexing Epirus to the Empire' in 1338.

region.text: Arta, Rogoi and Thomokastron, held by the rebels for Nikephoros II

ledger.note: Late 1338-1339: the Arta rebellion. 'At Catherine's instigation the Epirotes rebelled in Arta on behalf of Nikephoros in late 1338'; 'in the next year [they] rebelled against Palaiologan rule' (Monomachos page). Drawn as the despotate's land while the rebels hold it.

region.text: Arta, Rogoi and Thomokastron: 'by the end of the year, the various rebel-held strongholds capitulated'

ledger.note: 1340: the revolt collapses. Kantakouzenos 'persuaded the garrison to surrender' Thomokastron; 'Epirus returned to Byzantine control with John Angelos as governor'. The despotate is landless until 1356 (Serbian from 1348: Stefan Dusan 'had conquered Epirus in the late 1340s').

region.text: Thessaly and Epirus: Nikephoros 'took over the region in Spring 1356, and advanced on Epirus'

ledger.note: Spring 1356: Nikephoros II restores the despotate (infobox 'Restored by Nikephoros II Orsini: 1356'). From Ainos 'he sailed to Thessaly, which he captured quickly, expelling Preljub's wife and son' (Medieval Thessaly) and chased Simeon Uros from Arta.

region.text: Thessaly, 'taken over without resistance by Dusan's half-brother Simeon Uros'

ledger.note: 1359: Achelous. Nikephoros 'was killed in the Battle of Achelous in 1359' (the battle page: 'late spring or early summer of 1358 or 1359'); Simeon 'was welcomed and crowned by the local Greeks in Trikkala, with most of Thessaly following suit'.

region.text: 'Aetolia and southern Epirus were divided between' Pjeter Losha (Arta) and Gjin Bua Shpata (Angelokastron)

ledger.note: 1359: Epirus to the Albanian clans. Infobox: 'Albanians take control over Epirus, except Ioannina' and 'Re-establishment of Despotate of Arta' (established April 1359 per its own infobox; Losha at Arta, Shpata at Angelokastron, united 1374).

region.text: Ioannina, which 'remained under Greek governance' and submitted to Simeon Uros

ledger.note: 1359: Ioannina submits to Simeon Uros. 'Most of the major towns in the region ... quickly submitted to his rule'; he governed through deputies until he 'appointed Thomas Preljubovic'. The despotate is landless 1359-1366.

region.text: Ioannina and Vagenetia (Thesprotia), whose embassy Simeon forwarded to Thomas

ledger.note: 1367: the Despotate of Ioannina. 'Thomas arrived in Ioannina from Edessa in 1367 with a large army'; 'Simeon Uros responded by designating Thomas as his governor and forwarding the Ioanninan and Vagenetian (Thesprotian) embassy to him'. The Despotate page: in 1367 'Thomas II Preljubovic revived part of the despotate and kept Ioannina'.

region.text: 'Dryinopolis, Velas, Boursina, Krezounista, Dragomi and Vagenetia'

ledger.note: 1380-1381: Thomas on the offensive with Ottoman help. 'In 1380 Thomas passed to the offensive having also secured Ottoman support' and 'managed to expand his control in Dryinopolis, Velas, Boursina, Krezounista, Dragomi and Vagenetia'; the Mazreku of the Kalamas held out.

February 1385: Esau de' Buondelmonti. Thomas was 'assassinated in his bed by his own bodyguards' on 23 December 1384; Esau 'succeeded his captor by marrying the latter's widow, Maria Angelina Doukaina Palaiologina in February 1385'. He paid homage to Murad I in 1386 (Ottoman vassal tint from 1386, the Ottoman dossier's event).

region.text: 'much of his land was occupied by Zenebishi'

ledger.note: 1399: Esau captured. 'In 1399 Esau, supported by some Albanian clans, marched against his wife's brother-in-law' Gjon Zenebishi; 'Esau was routed and captured, and much of his land was occupied by Zenebishi'.

region.text: the Ioannina despotate's countryside

ledger.note: 1400: Esau returns to Ioannina. The page says he 'returned to Ioannina in 1400' and 'reigned on in relative peace'; the end of the Zenebishi occupation is the researcher's inference.

February 1411: the Tocco despotate. Esau died on 6 February 1411; Carlo I Tocco 'was invited as the successor of his uncle Esau de' Buondelmonti in Ioannina' 'after the rejection of the latter's widow and son in February 1411'; 'in 1415 he was granted the title despotes by the Byzantine Emperor Manuel II Palaiologos'.

region.text: the County Palatine of Cephalonia and Zakynthos with the duchy of Leukas (Lefkada), Carlo's since 1376

ledger.note: 1411: the Tocco islands and Ioannina united under one ruler. Carlo 'succeeded his father as count of Cephalonia and duke of Leukas on the latter's death in 1376'; Cliopatria ends its House of Tocco row in 1414 and adds the islands to Epirus in 1415.

region.text: Arta and the Acarnanian towns: 'now the Tocchi controlled all major towns in Epirus'

ledger.note: 4 October 1416: Arta surrenders (Despotate of Arta infobox 'Disestablished: 4 October 1416'). 'Carlo advanced on Arta and obtained its surrender in 1416'; 'In 1416, he defeated Jakob Bua Shpata and conquered Arta thus annexing the Despotate'. Angelokastro had been Carlo's 'from 1405' (a date the page marks dubious).

region.text: Glarentza, the port of Elis

ledger.note: 1421: Glarentza bought. Olivier Franco 'seized the town in 1418' from the Prince of Achaea and 'in 1421 he sold it to Carlo I Tocco'; 'in 1421 Carlo bought permanent possession of it from Oliverio Franco' (Carlo I page).

region.text: 'Glarentza and the other Moreot territories' of the Tocchi in Elis

ledger.note: 1 May 1428: Glarentza handed to Constantine Palaiologos. After the Byzantine naval victory at the Echinades (1427) Carlo's 'possessions were liquidated in a negotiated settlement'; 'Glarentza was given to the Byzantines on 1 May 1428 and on 1 July, Constantine married Theodora [Maddalena Tocco]'.

region.text: Ioannina

ledger.note: 9 October 1430: Ioannina surrenders to the Ottomans ('obtained the surrender of the city on October 9, 1430'). Carlo II 'continued to rule over the remnants of his principality in Epirus from Arta as an Ottoman vassal, while the illegitimate sons of his uncle received holdings in Acarnania as Ottoman dependents' (Ottoman vassal tint from 1430).
October 1430: the court moves to Arta.

region.text: Arta and 'all of Leonardo's mainland possessions, save for the three settlements of Vonitza, Varnazza and Angelokastro'

ledger.note: 24 March 1449: Arta falls. 'The capital of the despotate, Arta, fell to the Ottomans on 24 March 1449' and the mainland was annexed except three forts; the Tocco lands became the sanjak of Karli Ili.
1449: the court moves to Angelokastron (infobox 'Angelokastron (1449-60)').

region.text: Angelokastro and Varnazza, 'two out of his three fortresses on the mainland'

ledger.note: 1460: Angelokastron lost (Despotate page: 'Ottomans captured Angelokastron' 1460). 'Leonardo lost two out of his three fortresses on the mainland, only retaining Vonitza.'
1460: Vonitsa, the last mainland seat (infobox 'Vonitsa (1460-1479)'); Leonardo ruled from Lefkada.

region.text: Vonitsa and the islands of Lefkada, Cephalonia, Zakynthos and Ithaca

ledger.note: August-September 1479: the end. 'One-by-one, Leonardo's few remaining possessions quickly fell to the Ottomans in August and September 1479'; he 'fled from the island of Lefkada, where he had ruled from' to Taranto. Venice took Zakynthos in 1482 and Cephalonia for good after 1500.

region.text: the last Tocco possessions, Vonitsa and the Ionian islands

ledger.note: 1479: the Despotate of Epirus ends with the Ottoman capture of Vonitsa (infobox 'Ottoman conquest of Vonitsa: 1479'). Cliopatria's row runs to 1481.

wars.name: Epirote conquest of Thessaly and Thessalonica

zones.text: Larissa 1212, Platamon 1218, the rest except Halmyros c. 1222

wars.outcome: Epirote victory: Michael I took Thessaly in 1212; Theodore 'gradually conquered all of Thessalonica except the city itself' over nine years and took the city in December 1224; Peter of Courtenay captured 1217.

wars.name: Theodore's Thracian campaign

zones.text: Christopolis, Xanthi, Mosynopolis, Didymoteicho, Adrianople; Bizye and Vrysis reached

wars.outcome: Theodore took western Thrace from the Latins and Adrianople from the Nicaeans; 'Constantinople itself was not attacked'; a truce with the Latins in 1228.

wars.name: Battle of Klokotnitsa
wars.outcome: Bulgarian victory on 9 March 1230; Theodore captured and blinded; Thrace, most of Macedonia and Albania Bulgarian; Thessalonica a Bulgarian vassal under Manuel; Epirus proper independent under Michael II.

wars.name: Epirote-Nicaean war of 1251-1253
wars.outcome: Nicaean victory: the treaty of Larissa (1252) ceded all Epirote holdings in Macedonia and put Kruja under Nicaean suzerainty; Vodena, Kastoria and Deabolis taken in winter 1252/53.

wars.name: Epirote-Nicaean conflict (1257-1259) and the Battle of Pelagonia

zones.text: Dyrrhachium and the Adriatic forts, Manfred's from February 1258

wars.outcome: Nicaean victory at Pelagonia (summer or autumn 1259): 'Collapse of the Epiroto-Latin League'; Arta taken and Ioannina besieged, then 'the Nicaean successes were largely undone' in 1260; Manfred kept Corfu and Albania; Michael II accepted Michael VIII's nominal suzerainty in 1264.
wars.note: The article 'Epirote-Nicaean conflict (1257-59)' would not load under either title tried; the Pelagonia, Theodore II Laskaris and Michael II pages carry the dates.

wars.name: Angevin-Byzantine war in Albania

zones.text: the Albanian holdings lost to the Byzantines after 1279

wars.outcome: Charles of Anjou took Dyrrhachium in 1272; the Byzantine campaign of 1274 (Byzantine forces re-entered Butrint) 'infringed on Nikephoros' interests' and he allied with Charles in 1276; the coalition of Charles, Nikephoros and John I Doukas drove the Byzantines out of Butrint in 1278; in 1279 Nikephoros became Charles' vassal and surrendered it; after Charles' defeat he 'lost his holdings in Albania to the Byzantines'.

wars.name: Angevin-Epirote war of 1304-1307
wars.outcome: Epirus recovered Butrint and Naupaktos in 1304-1305; the Angevin invasion of 1307 'ended with a compromise' returning many fortresses to Philip of Taranto, who gave up his claim in 1312.

wars.name: Byzantine annexation of Epirus
wars.outcome: Byzantine victory: Epirus annexed 1337/1338; the Arta revolt of late 1338 crushed by the end of 1340 ('the various rebel-held strongholds capitulated'); John Angelos governor.

wars.name: Battle of Achelous (1359)

zones.text: Aetolia and southern Epirus, divided between Losha and Shpata

wars.outcome: Albanian victory; Nikephoros II killed; 'Albanians take control over Epirus, except Ioannina'; Despotate of Arta re-established; Thessaly to Simeon Uros.

wars.name: Albanian-Epirote wars of Ioannina

zones.text: Arta, surrendered to Carlo I Tocco 4 October 1416

wars.outcome: Thomas Preljubovic (with Ottoman help from 1380) and Esau held Ioannina against Losha and the Shpata; Esau was captured by Zenebishi in 1399; Carlo I Tocco 'finally managed to subdue the Albanian clans and seized Arta in 1416'.

wars.name: Tocco-Byzantine war in the Morea

zones.text: Glarentza and the Tocco lands in Elis

wars.outcome: Byzantine victory at the Echinades (1427), 'the last in the Empire's naval history'; Glarentza and the Moreot lands handed over as Maddalena Tocco's dowry on 1 May 1428.

wars.name: Ottoman conquest of the Tocco despotate
wars.outcome: Ottoman conquest in stages: Ioannina 1430, Arta and the mainland 1449, Angelokastro 1460, Vonitsa and the Ionian islands 1479; Leonardo III fled to Taranto.

certainty.note: Medieval Balkan frontiers held by towns and castles; no treaty line is recorded except the 1252 Larissa treaty's cession of named towns. The Achelous was the Epirus-Thessaly border after 1268 (John I Doukas page). Island coasts are sharp.

notes:
Cliopatria rows: the Despotate of Epirus row (1206-1481) begins a year late (1205) and ends two years late (1479). Its 1227-1235 shape keeps Theodore's Thessalonican empire whole for five years after Klokotnitsa (9 March 1230) while the Empire of Thessalonica row starts only in 1236; this dossier carries the 1224-1230 empire as a rename (rule 2) and splits the Thessalonican rump off in 1230, so the sibling empire-of-thessalonica dossier starts in 1230 with new keyframes to 1235 (Wikipedia's own start for the Empire of Thessalonica is 1224; the Epirus infobox lists the Empire of Thessalonica as both predecessor and successor). The 1250-1271 shape keeps northern Albania Epirote to 1271 although Dyrrhachium and Servia went to Nicaea in 1256 (Dyrrhachium passing on to Manfred in February 1258), Valona and Butrint to Manfred in 1258 and Corfu with Helena's dowry in 1259; the 1272-1278 shape still contains Valona, Berat and Butrint, which the ledger says Epirus did not hold then (Butrint Angevin 1267, Byzantine 1274-1278), and is left as Cliopatria has it. Review repairs of 2026-10-19: the 1278 Butrint gain is from the Byzantines, not from Charles (Butrint page); the 1258 loss no longer includes Dyrrhachium; the 1259 losses of Ohrid, Deavolis and Prilep to Nicaea were added (the Prilep one at confidence 1, the Pelagonia page being silent on it). Thessaly left the despotate in 1267/68 (Cliopatria's Thessaly row starts 1272). Cliopatria has no Epirote shape 1344-1384: the state was Byzantine 1340-1348 and Serbian 1348-1356, restored by Nikephoros II 1356-1359 (new keyframe), Albanian except Ioannina after Achelous, and revived at Ioannina by Thomas Preljubovic from 1367 (new keyframe); Cliopatria's Despotate of Arta row (1375-1421, a sibling) carries the Albanian south. From 1415 Cliopatria folds the Tocco county of Cephalonia (its House of Tocco row ends 1414) into Epirus; this dossier records the union in February 1411. The 1431 shape should begin in October 1430 and the 1450 shape in March 1449; the 1459 shape a year early (Angelokastro fell 1460).

Gaps (confidence 1): the previous holder of Ohrid-Prilep-Pelagonia in 1216-1217 and of the Albanian and Macedonian towns taken in 1246; the date Kruja/Arbanon was absorbed; which fortresses were in Thamar's 1294 dowry (Naupaktos, Vonitsa, Butrint are the reading); whether and when John II Orsini recovered Ioannina (1318 loss is on the page; a 1325 recovery is inferred from 'all of Epirus' and from Ioannina being Byzantine again by 1335); the end of the Zenebishi occupation (1400). Pages that would not load: 'Epirote-Nicaean conflict (1257-59)' under both URL spellings. Disagreements between pages: Adrianople retaken 1225 (Despotate page) or 1227 (Vatatzes page); Theodore's coronation 1225 or 29 May 1227; Byzantine conquest 1337 (infobox) or Arta 1338 (Monomachos page); Achelous 1358 or 1359; Carlo II's death 30 September (Leonardo III page) or October 1448 (Carlo II page); Michael II's death 1266/68.

States that need dossiers from other groups: Principality of Arbanon (c. 1190-c. 1255, Kruja; no Cliopatria row seen) as counterpart of the c. 1215 gain; the Despotate of Angelokastron and Lepanto (Shpata, c. 1360-1406/07) is covered by the sibling despotate-of-arta row after 1374. Vassal relations for the rendering agents (rule 4, recorded by the suzerain's dossier): Epirus a Venetian vassal 1210 (Michael I's treaty), Charles of Anjou's 1279-1281, Byzantine 1264 and c. 1324-1337 (nominal), Angevin 1331, Ottoman from 1386 (Esau's homage) and 1430 (Carlo II). Gazetteer names used as coordinates because the gazetteer lacks them: Arta, Vonitsa, Angelokastro, Naupaktos, Butrint, Platamon, Halmyros, Servia, Kastoria, Vodena (Edessa), Veles, Rogoi, Didymoteicho, Glarentza, Cephalonia, Zakynthos, Lefkada; Dryinopolis is drawn around Gjirokaster.
